Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff consumer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A collection letter that the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read in two ways, one of them inaccurate, violates the FDCPA.

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act forbids a debt collector from using "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt," including the "false representation of the character, amount, or legal status of any debt" and any "false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e, (2)(A), (10). This Court has long measured those prohibitions by the understanding of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Graziano v. Harrison*, 950 F.2d 107, 111 (3d Cir. 1991); *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000). The standard protects "the gullible as well as the shrewd" and ensures that the Act safeguards "all consumers, the shrewd as well as the ingenuous." *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006). It also guards debt collectors against liability for "bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations" of their letters. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. The least sophisticated debtor is presumed to have "a basic level of understanding and willingness to read with care." *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298–99 (3d Cir. 2008).

Applying that standard, this Court has held that a collection letter is deceptive "when it can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 222 (3d Cir. 2008); *accord Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455; *Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 149 (3d Cir. 2013). Under this rule, a collector cannot defend a letter by pointing to one accurate reading when another reasonable reading is false. The question is not what the collector intended or what a sophisticated lawyer would understand. The question is whether the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably take the letter to say something untrue. *See Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. Because the Act is a strict-liability statute as to the collector's misrepresentations, the collector bears the risk of ambiguity it created. *See Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011).

The inquiry is objective, and it does not require proof that the plaintiff was actually confused. *See Douglass v. Convergent Outsourcing*, 765 F.3d 299, 303 (3d Cir. 2014). It does require that the plaintiff's reading be reasonable and not fanciful. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. The alternative reading must also concern a material fact, meaning one capable of influencing the debtor's decision about how to respond to the collection effort. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 421 (3d Cir. 2015).

### II. The [Date] letter satisfies this test.

The letter can reasonably be read in two ways. [Describe the letter's language and the accurate reading, with record cites.] But a least sophisticated debtor could just as reasonably read the same language to mean that [describe the inaccurate reading, e.g., that the balance is fixed, that the offer expires, or that a particular consequence will follow]. [Explain why the second reading is not bizarre or idiosyncratic, relying on the letter's wording, layout, and context.] That second reading is inaccurate because [state the actual facts, e.g., interest and fees continue to accrue, no such consequence is intended or permitted].

The inaccuracy is material under *Jensen*. A debtor who believed [the inaccurate reading] would be likely to [pay, ignore, or delay a response, or forgo a right], and so would be misled about [the amount, status, or consequences of the debt]. *See Jensen*, 791 F.3d at 421. This is the harm that § 1692e is meant to prevent.

Defendant cannot escape liability because the letter also supports an accurate reading. *Rosenau* and *Brown* reject that defense. Under the "two or more meanings" rule, the existence of a truthful reading does not cure a reasonable misleading one. *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 222; *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455. Nor does it matter that Defendant may not have intended the misleading meaning. Defendant chose the words, and the Act places the burden of clarity on the collector. The District Court's contrary conclusion should be reversed.
